en: Are you feeling dizzy or weak?
tamil: உங்களுக்கு தலை சுத்துதா இல்ல சோர்வா இருக்கா?
context: A doctor asking about symptoms.
explain: 'Dizzy' means the head feels like spinning. 'Or' offers two symptoms to choose from.
usage: A doctor or a nurse asks this at a check-up.
leelaQ: How do you feel when you are very tired?
answer: I feel weak, and I cannot focus on my work.

en: Where does it hurt exactly?
tamil: சரியா எங்க வலிக்குது?
context: A doctor asking about pain.
explain: 'Exactly' asks for the exact spot. 'Hurt' is a verb for pain.
usage: A doctor or physiotherapist asks this to find the pain.
leelaQ: Can you show where you had pain last time?
answer: I had pain in my lower back, near the waist.

en: Did you eat anything unusual last night?
tamil: நேத்து ராத்திரி ஏதாவது வித்தியாசமா சாப்பிட்டீங்களா?
context: A doctor asking about stomach trouble.
explain: 'Anything unusual' means something not normal. 'Did you eat ...?' asks about the past.
usage: Doctors ask this when a patient has stomach pain or loose motion.
leelaQ: What did you eat for dinner yesterday?
answer: I ate chapati and dal with a little rice.

en: When should I come back for the next check-up?
tamil: அடுத்த செக்-அப்புக்கு நான் எப்போ திரும்ப வரணும்?
context: Asking a doctor before leaving.
explain: 'Come back' means return. 'Should I' asks for the doctor's advice.
usage: Ask this at the end of a visit to the doctor.
leelaQ: What do you ask the doctor before leaving the room?
answer: I ask about the food rules and the next visit date.

en: Do you do any exercise at home?
tamil: நீங்க வீட்டுல ஏதாவது உடற்பயிற்சி பண்றீங்களா?
context: A doctor or friend asking about your lifestyle.
explain: 'Do you do ...?' asks about a habit. 'Any' makes the question open.
usage: A doctor or a trainer asks this to learn about your lifestyle.
leelaQ: Do you do any exercise at home? Which one?
answer: Yes, I do simple stretching for ten minutes every morning.

en: Will I need an injection?
tamil: எனக்கு ஊசி போடணுமா?
context: Asking a doctor, a bit nervously.
explain: 'Will I need ...?' asks if something will be required. It is short and polite.
usage: Say it to a doctor or a nurse when you feel afraid.
leelaQ: Are you afraid of injections? Why?
answer: Yes, a little, because I do not like the pain.

en: What did the doctor say about your report?
tamil: உங்க ரிப்போர்ட் பத்தி டாக்டர் என்ன சொன்னாரு?
context: Asking a friend or relative after their visit.
explain: 'What did ... say' asks about past words. The verb 'say' stays in base form.
usage: Use it with a friend or family member who went for a test.
leelaQ: How do you feel when you wait for a test result?
answer: I feel nervous until the doctor says everything is normal.

en: How is your father's health now?
tamil: உங்க அப்பாவோட உடம்பு இப்போ எப்படி இருக்கு?
context: Asking about a colleague's family member.
explain: 'How is ... now?' is a polite way to ask about recovery. 'Health' is a noun.
usage: Use it in an office or neighbourhood when you care about someone.
leelaQ: How is your family's health these days?
answer: Everyone is fine, thank God, and we are all busy.

en: Please open your mouth and say aaah.
tamil: வாயைத் திறந்து ஆஹ்னு சொல்லுங்க.
context: A doctor checking your throat.
explain: Two imperatives are joined with 'and'. Doctors use simple commands like this.
usage: Doctors say this during a throat check-up.
leelaQ: What does a doctor check first when you have a cold?
answer: He checks my throat, my nose and my temperature.

en: Could you speak a little slower, doctor?
tamil: கொஞ்சம் மெதுவா பேச முடியுமா டாக்டர்?
context: Asking a doctor to repeat clearly.
explain: 'A little slower' is a soft way to ask. 'Could you' makes it polite.
usage: Use it when someone speaks fast and you cannot follow.
leelaQ: What do you do when you do not understand something?
answer: I ask the person to repeat it slowly.

en: Breathe in slowly and then breathe out.
tamil: மெதுவா மூச்சை உள்ள இழுத்து அப்புறம் வெளியே விடுங்க.
context: A doctor listening to your chest.
explain: 'Breathe in' and 'breathe out' are phrasal verbs. 'Slowly' tells how to do it.
usage: Doctors, nurses and yoga teachers give this instruction.
leelaQ: When do you take deep breaths?
answer: I take deep breaths when I feel stressed or angry.

en: Can you take me to the hospital right now?
tamil: நீ இப்போவே என்னை ஆஸ்பத்திரிக்கு கூட்டிட்டுப் போக முடியுமா?
context: Asking a family member in an urgent case.
explain: 'Right now' shows urgency. 'Take me to' means to go with me and drop me.
usage: Say it to family or a neighbour in an emergency.
leelaQ: Who will you call if you need help at night?
answer: I will call my brother or a neighbour who has a car.

en: I do not eat non-veg food during fasting days.
tamil: நான் விரத நாட்கள்ல அசைவம் சாப்பிட மாட்டேன்.
context: Explaining a food rule to a colleague.
explain: 'Do not eat' is a present negative. 'Non-veg' is a short form of non-vegetarian.
usage: Use it politely when someone offers you food on a fasting day.
leelaQ: What food do you avoid and why?
answer: I avoid very spicy food because it upsets my stomach.

en: I have never taken any sleeping pills.
tamil: நான் இதுவரைக்கும் தூக்க மாத்திரை எடுத்ததே இல்ல.
context: Telling a doctor about your history.
explain: 'Have never taken' talks about your whole life up to now. 'Any' stresses none.
usage: Say it when a doctor asks about medicines you took before.
leelaQ: What natural way do you use to fall asleep?
answer: I drink warm milk and listen to soft music.

en: I get a headache whenever I sit before the computer too long.
tamil: கம்ப்யூட்டர் முன்னாடி ரொம்ப நேரம் உக்கார்ந்தா எனக்கு தலைவலி வரும்.
context: Explaining your problem to a doctor.
explain: 'Whenever' means every time. It joins a habit and its result.
usage: Use it with a doctor or an optician when you describe your problem.
leelaQ: Do you work on a computer? How do you rest your eyes?
answer: Yes, I look away for a minute after every hour.

en: It is only a mild infection, so there is nothing to worry about.
tamil: இது சின்ன இன்ஃபெக்ஷன் தான், அதனால கவலைப்பட ஒண்ணும் இல்ல.
context: A doctor calming a patient.
explain: 'Mild' means not serious. 'Nothing to worry about' is a comforting phrase.
usage: Doctors or elders use it to comfort someone who is anxious.
leelaQ: What do you say to a person who is worried about health?
answer: I tell them to relax and follow the doctor's advice.

en: I stayed in bed the whole day because of the fever.
tamil: காய்ச்சல் காரணமா நான் நாள் முழுக்க படுக்கையிலேயே இருந்தேன்.
context: Telling a friend why you did not call.
explain: 'Because of' is followed by a noun. 'The whole day' means all day.
usage: Use it to explain why you missed work or a call.
leelaQ: What do you do on a day when you are sick?
answer: I rest at home, drink hot soup and watch some TV.

en: The pain has reduced a lot after the injection.
tamil: ஊசி போட்டதுக்கு அப்புறம் வலி ரொம்ப குறைஞ்சிடுச்சு.
context: Telling the doctor how you feel.
explain: 'Has reduced' shows a change with a result now. 'A lot' means very much.
usage: Say it in a follow-up visit or when family asks about your health.
leelaQ: How do you feel when your pain goes away?
answer: I feel relaxed and happy, and I start doing my work again.

en: My neighbour is a doctor, so we ask him for small problems.
tamil: எங்க பக்கத்து வீட்டுக்காரர் டாக்டர், அதனால சின்ன பிரச்சனைனா அவர் கிட்ட கேப்போம்.
context: Talking about a helpful neighbour.
explain: 'So' joins a reason and a result. 'Small problems' means minor health issues.
usage: Use it in a talk about community and support.
leelaQ: Do you have a helpful neighbour? How do they help?
answer: Yes, my neighbour helps us when we need a lift or a tool.

en: I will ask my wife to prepare light food for dinner.
tamil: நான் ராத்திரிக்கு லேசான சாப்பாடு செய்யச் சொல்லி என் மனைவிகிட்ட கேக்கறேன்.
context: Telling a doctor or friend about diet changes.
explain: 'Will ask ... to ...' shows a plan. 'Light food' means easy-to-digest food.
usage: Use it when you plan to eat simple food after an illness.
leelaQ: What light food do you eat when you are sick?
answer: I eat rice porridge or idli with a little chutney.

en: Many people in my office have caught the viral fever.
tamil: எங்க ஆபீஸ்ல நிறைய பேருக்கு வைரல் காய்ச்சல் பிடிச்சிருக்கு.
context: Telling a friend about an illness at work.
explain: 'Have caught' is used with a fever or cold. 'Many people' is a plural subject.
usage: Use it when you talk about a seasonal illness.
leelaQ: What do you do to stay safe in the rainy season?
answer: I drink boiled water and avoid street food.

en: I am going to take two days' leave for my health.
tamil: நான் என் உடம்புக்காக ரெண்டு நாள் லீவு எடுக்கப் போறேன்.
context: Telling a manager you need rest.
explain: 'Am going to take' shows a plan. 'Leave' means a break from work.
usage: Say it to a manager, a teacher or a friend when you need rest.
leelaQ: Do you take leave when you are not well?
answer: Yes, I take one or two days so that I can recover fully.

en: Walking after dinner helps with digestion.
tamil: சாப்பிட்ட பிறகு நடந்தா செரிமானம் நல்லா இருக்கும்.
context: Giving a health tip to a friend.
explain: 'Walking' acts as a noun here. 'Helps with' shows the benefit.
usage: Use it as friendly advice in a talk about health.
leelaQ: Do you walk after dinner? For how long?
answer: Yes, I walk for fifteen minutes near my house.

en: My sister is waiting outside the doctor's room.
tamil: என் தங்கை டாக்டர் ரூமுக்கு வெளியே காத்துட்டு இருக்கா.
context: Telling a nurse who is with you.
explain: 'Is waiting' shows an action in progress. 'Outside' tells the place.
usage: Say it at a hospital to explain who has come with you.
leelaQ: Who comes with you when you visit a hospital?
answer: My sister usually comes with me and carries my file.

en: Health is more important than money, so take care.
tamil: உடம்பு தான் பணத்தை விட முக்கியம், அதனால பாத்துக்கோங்க.
context: Advising a friend who works too much.
explain: 'More ... than' compares two things. 'Take care' is a warm closing phrase.
usage: Use it kindly with a friend who ignores their health.
leelaQ: What is more important to you, health or money? Why?
answer: Health is more important, because I need it for everything.
